extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of poetry; literary critics; creative-writing students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reading, judging, and writing lyrical poetry with attention to sentimentality, coherence, doctrine, belief, and sincerity. Emphasises close reading and distinguishing emotional vs intellectual responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentimentality — quantitative sense (excess of feeling)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poem is the product of a mind which was too easily stirred to emotion; it came about through facile feelings; the author was himself sentimental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish whether the author produced excessive emotion (Sense One) versus whether readers would be too easily moved by the poem. Example: charges that a poem shows 'over-production of emotion' or that the poet 'revels in emotion for its own sake.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentimentality — crudeness sense (undirected, crude feeling)
rubrics_metrics.description: A crude, undirected, objectless feeling of pathos that attaches itself to anything that will give it an excuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for emotional responses enjoyed for their own sake, 'luxuriated in' without attachment to a concrete object or situation. Such crude response is often produced by pooled, incoherent decorative items or conventional trappings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentimentality — inappropriateness to situation (third sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: A response is sentimental when, either through the over-persistence of tendencies or through the interaction of sentiments, it is inappropriate to the situation that calls it forth — by confining itself to one aspect only or by substituting a factitious, illusory situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect when feeling is confined to a stereotyped, unrepresentative aspect of the prompting situation (e.g., idealised childhood or glorified war). Examples: nostalgia for war or school-days that ignores other aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish authorial sentimentality from readerly susceptibility
rubrics_metrics.description: When calling a poem 'sentimental' we may mean that the author was sentimental or that readers would be too easily moved (we should distinguish the two).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid conflating these claims; sometimes only the latter is warranted. Compare with sincerity and determine whether excess arises from the poet's shaping impulses or from readers' stock responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat lyric as semi-dramatic utterance (correct approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lyrical, emotional verse should be taken as a semi-dramatic utterance not inviting ironical contemplation — to be judged on its merits as poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not read such verses as sociological realism or attempt to render them as realistic social documents. Take the speaker's words and cadences as part of the situation presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feeling must be founded in the presented situation (concreteness requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The situation must be concrete enough, near enough, and coherent enough to justify the vigorous emotional response invited from us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An abstract theme in itself cannot justify any extremity of sympathetic emotion. Ask: is the situation as given concrete/coherent/near to us? If not, the emotional claim is suspect (cf. Gray’s Elegy as counterexample).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression should be dictated by feeling, not feeling led by expressive facilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid poems where facilities and conveniences of expression indicate that expression has led feeling rather than feeling dictating expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for mechanical structure, conspicuous rhymes, antitheses, or other 'facilities' that suggest emotions worked up for their own sake or to achieve effects ('trying to get effects the whole time').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conventional, borrowed, second‑hand metaphors that undermine concreteness and coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: Borrowed decorations and conventional metaphors often fail in nearness and concreteness and tend to be irrelevant, producing incoherence in the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If decorative items do not hang together or reflect a second-hand quality, they may indicate weakness in the central impulse of the poem. Such conventionality may explain popularity but can justify rejection when it reflects weakness of the thing expressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence of imagery and elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Various items in a poem must 'hang together' — their combined effect should be directed, not crude or undirected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether images (sunshine, dog-roses, winter, wind, etc.) fit together logically and emotionally; incoherent pooling of images produces undirected pathos and crude response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of abstracted themes as excuses for extreme emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: An abstract theme (e.g., 'a girl bewailing her lost lover') is nothing in itself and cannot in itself excuse any emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the concreteness and particularity of the situation presented — the poet must present particulars (every word, cadence, movement) that make the emotion appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Close reading required before judging sentimentality
rubrics_metrics.description: Before deciding whether a poem is or is not sentimental we must be sure that we know both what the presented situation is and what response is invited — only the very closest reading will tell us enough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid snap judgments based on surface readings or stock impressions; protocol examples show misreadings of situation lead to mistaken accusations of sentimentality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect enjoyment of emotion for its own sake (emotion as an end)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the emotion can be concocted by the reader without the poem, and is enjoyable for its own sake regardless of object, it indicates sentimentality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether readers can 'sit down by the fireside and concoct a precisely similar emotion' merely by saying 'Oh!' in tones of sadness — such self-enjoyment signals sentimentality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of sentimental distortion — expansion vs destruction
rubrics_metrics.description: The cure for mawkish attachment is to take the distorted sentiment and work it into close and living relation with some scene concretely and truthfully realised (treatment by expansion); sneers/realism aimed at destroying the response are ineffective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer enlarging and integrating the canalised response rather than attempting to dry it up by caustics, which may increase impoverishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inhibition as source of sentimental fixations
rubrics_metrics.description: Most sentimental fixations and distortions of feeling are the result of inhibitions — permanent curtailment of possibilities through repeated maintained inhibition blanks out aspects of experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for avoidance of painful aspects of life; sentimentality often replaces painful aspects with pleasant ones or factitious objects. Also note social controls and fashions (e.g., attitudes to tears) that shape publicly avowable sentiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of interest (breadth of response)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sentimentalist is not distributing his interest widely enough and is distributing it in too few forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the poem (or reader) is canalising attention into a narrow set of stereotyped responses rather than encompassing a wider range of experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish intellectual belief from emotional belief
rubrics_metrics.description: Intellectual belief is a 'loading' of ideas into a logical system; emotional belief is acceptance of an idea insofar as it serves needs and emotional activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poem may invite emotional belief without requiring intellectual assent; understanding the difference helps avoid false charges of insincerity or claims that doctrinal agreement is necessary for poetic response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion: does the poem require intellectual assent to be read as poetry?
rubrics_metrics.description: If the question of intellectual belief arises (i.e., one is forced into theological/astronomical/moral debate), one has ceased to be reading poetry in the poetic mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good reading often prevents the intellectual-belief question from arising; where it does, the poem's execution or the reader's approach may be at fault. Many readers give full emotional belief while withholding intellectual belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity — correspondence between poem's claim and poet's shaping impulses
rubrics_metrics.description: Insincerity (in the critical sense used here) is a discrepancy between the poem’s claim upon our response and its shaping impulses in the poet’s mind; not merely deliberate deception but mismatch of motive and expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poem may be produced for money, pique or ambition and still be good provided external motives do not interfere with its growth. Usual causes of this insincerity: desire to be 'original', 'striking', or 'poetic'. Note: irony need not be insincere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification of emotional belief — prudence and meeting needs
rubrics_metrics.description: An emotional belief is justified only by its success in meeting our needs; its desirability has nothing to do with its intellectual status provided it does not interfere with the intellectual system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the emotional acceptance facilitated by the poem prudently serves the reader's wider needs and does not harm intellectual functioning.
